antoni_gaudi.name: Antoni Gaudí
antoni_gaudi.full_name: Antoni Plàcid Guillem Gaudí i Cornet
antoni_gaudi.born: 25 June 1852, in Reus (or possibly neighbouring Riudoms; his exact birthplace is disputed), Catalonia, Spain
antoni_gaudi.died: 10 June 1926 (age 73), in Barcelona, three days after being hit by a tram on 7 June 1926
antoni_gaudi.style: Catalan Modernisme (Art Nouveau); considered its greatest exponent, though his mature work transcends the movement, drawing chiefly from natural and geometric forms (ruled surfaces, hyperboloids, catenary arches)
antoni_gaudi.education: Barcelona Higher School of Architecture, graduated 1878
antoni_gaudi.religious_note: Devout Catholic, nicknamed "God's Architect"; his cause for canonisation opened in 2003, and Pope Francis authorised his declaration as Venerable on 14 April 2025; he has not yet reached beatification
antoni_gaudi.unesco_status: Seven works declared UNESCO World Heritage Sites under 'Works of Antoni Gaudí': 1984 original listing (Park Güell, Palau Güell, Casa Milà) and 2005 extension (Nativity façade and crypt of Sagrada Família, Casa Vicens, Casa Batlló, crypt of Colònia Güell)
antoni_gaudi.burial: Buried in the crypt of the Sagrada Família, which he devoted the last years of his life to
notable_facts: Never married; devoted his life entirely to his profession and, from 1915 onward, to the Sagrada Família alone
Rarely drew detailed plans, preferring three-dimensional scale models he shaped as he conceived a design

Died after being struck by a Barcelona tram on 7 June 1926 while walking to daily prayer and confession; because of his shabby dress in later life he was initially mistaken for a beggar and did not receive immediate aid, dying three days later on 10 June 1926
His principal patron was industrialist Eusebi Güell, who commissioned Park Güell, Palau Güell, and the crypt of Colònia Güell, among other major works
Influenced later architects including Le Corbusier, Pier Luigi Nervi, Friedensreich Hundertwasser, Oscar Niemeyer, Félix Candela, Eduardo Torroja, Santiago Calatrava, and Norman Foster

On 11 September 1924 (Catalonia's National Day), Gaudí was beaten at a demonstration against the Catalan language ban and arrested by the Civil Guard while travelling to attend a mass for Catalan patriots; he refused to speak Spanish, insisting he paid his taxes but would not stop speaking his own language, and was released after paying 50 pesetas bail

Introduced the trencadís mosaic technique using broken or waste ceramic pieces, seen on the undulating bench at Park Güell (with Josep Maria Jujol) and the façade of Casa Batlló (with waste from the Pelegrí glassworks)

Emili Sala Cortés was one of Gaudí's professors at the Barcelona architecture school, and Gaudí worked as a draughtsman for him early in his career to help finance his studies; decades later Gaudí was hired to completely redesign Sala Cortés's original 1877 building into Casa Batlló

Dragons were seen as Catalan nationalist symbols during the Renaixença due to their connection with Saint George (patron saint of Catalonia), connecting Casa Batlló's dragon-back roof and Park Güell's dragon/salamander to Gaudí's Catalan identity

sagrada_familia.name: Sagrada Família
sagrada_familia.full_name: Basílica i Temple Expiatori de la Sagrada Família
aliases: temple expiatori de la sagrada familia
sagrada_familia.architect: Antoni Gaudí (took over from Francisco de Paula del Villar after Villar's resignation on 18 March 1883 due to disagreements with the construction board; Gaudí was formally appointed Architect Director on 28 March 1884 and redesigned the project, keeping only the crypt)
sagrada_familia.style: Gothic Revival combined with curvilinear Art Nouveau / Catalan Modernisme
sagrada_familia.height: 172.5 m (566 ft); reached its final height on 20 February 2026 with completion of the central Jesus Christ tower, making it the tallest church in the world
sagrada_familia.consecrated: 7 November 2010, by Pope Benedict XVI, who proclaimed it a minor basilica
sagrada_familia.unesco_status: The Nativity façade and Crypt were added to the existing (1984) 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' UNESCO World Heritage Site listing in 2005
sagrada_familia.status: Still under construction. On 30 October 2025 it became the tallest church building in the world, surpassing Ulm Minster (161.5 m); it reached its full height of 172.5 m on 20 February 2026. The main structure was targeted for completion around 2026 (the centenary of Gaudí's death), but sculptural details, decoration, and a planned monumental stairway are expected to continue until 2034. Funded solely by private donations and visitor entry fees, with no government or church funding. Received 3 million visitors by 1990 and 5 million in 2025.
notable_facts: As of 30 October 2025, it is the tallest church in the world (172.5 m, ~11 m taller than the former record-holder, Ulm Minster)
Gaudí devoted the rest of his life to the project and is buried in its crypt
At Gaudí's death in 1926, only an estimated 15-25% of the project was complete
In July 1936, anarchists from the FAI set fire to the crypt during the Spanish Civil War and broke into Gaudí's workshop, destroying many of his original plans and models

An arsonist set a small fire in the sacristy in April 2011; investigations later revealed the basilica was an intended target of the 2017 Barcelona (La Rambla) terrorist attacks, a plot that was abandoned after an accidental explosion at the attackers' bomb-making site
Construction halted for the first time since the Civil War when COVID-19 closed the site in March 2020

The interior columns are a unique Gaudí design that branch to support their load, with ever-changing cross-sections created by intersecting geometric forms — for example, a square base evolving into an octagon, then a sixteen-sided shape, and eventually a circle, produced by two helicoidal columns twisting in opposite directions

An organ with 26 stops and 1,492 pipes on two manuals and a pedalboard was installed in the chancel in 2010 by Blancafort Orgueners de Montserrat; additional organs are planned throughout the building, totaling around 8,000 pipes when complete

The Passion façade contains a magic square based on the 1514 print Melencolia I by Albrecht Dürer, modified so its rows, columns, and diagonals add up to 33 (Christ's age at death) instead of the standard 34 for a 4x4 magic square

The central doors of the Glory façade, designed by Josep Maria Subirachs and installed in September 2008, bear the text of the Lord's Prayer in Catalan in high relief, surrounded by the phrase 'give us this day our daily bread' in fifty other languages; the door handles form the letters 'A' and 'G' for Antoni Gaudí

casa_batllo.name: Casa Batlló
casa_batllo.location: Passeig de Gràcia, Eixample district, Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain (part of the 'Illa de la Discòrdia' / 'Block of Discord', a row of four houses by leading Modernista architects in rivalry)
casa_batllo.architect: Antoni Gaudí, assisted by Domènec Sugrañes i Gras, Josep Canaleta, and Joan Rubió (renovation of an existing 1877 eclectic building originally commissioned by Lluís Sala Sánchez and designed by Emili Sala Cortés, one of Gaudí's professors)
casa_batllo.commissioned_by: Josep Batlló i Casanovas, a textile industrialist, who bought the original house in 1903 and hired Gaudí in 1904 (who had already been chief architect of Sagrada Família for 20 years) to outdo neighbours in the Illa de la Discòrdia rivalry
casa_batllo.construction_start: 1904 (design and renovation began; Gaudí convinced Batlló to renovate rather than demolish and rebuild)
casa_batllo.unesco_status: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' (reference 320-006); the overall listing was inscribed in 1984 and extended in 2005 to include Casa Batlló
casa_batllo.status: Completed, open to the public as a museum
notable_facts: The façade is covered in colorful trencadís (broken tile mosaic) made from waste ceramic from the Pelegrí glassworks
Locally nicknamed 'Casa dels ossos' (House of Bones) for its skeletal, organic façade; also informally called the 'house of yawns' for the rounded mouth-like shapes around its main floor windows
The arched roof is popularly interpreted as the back of a dragon, with a turret and cross said to represent Saint George's lance plunged into it; Saint George is the patron saint of Catalonia
Became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005
The Batlló family lived on the main floor until the mid-1950s; the current owners bought the building in 1993 and opened it to the public in 2002

The central part of the façade evokes the rippling surface of a lake with water lilies, reminiscent of Monet's Nymphéas paintings, covered with plaster fragments of colored glass discs combined with 330 rounds of polychrome pottery, designed by Gaudí and Josep Maria Jujol while working in Majorca on the Palma Cathedral

The loft of Casa Batlló contains sixty catenary arches forming a ribcage-like structure that distributes weight evenly with self-cancelling tangential forces, supporting loads without external buttresses
The roof terrace is decorated with four chimney stacks designed with specialized curves to prevent backdraughts

park_guell.name: Park Güell
park_guell.location: La Salut neighbourhood, Gràcia district, Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain, on the southern slope of Turó del Carmel hill (part of the Collserola mountain range), on a rocky site originally known as Muntanya Pelada (Bare Mountain)
park_guell.architect: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Eusebi Güell; the curving mosaic bench was designed by Josep Maria Jujol
park_guell.style: Catalan Modernisme, blending Arts and Crafts, Symbolism, Expressionism, and Rationalism influences
park_guell.construction_end: 1914 (construction complete); the park officially opened to the public in 1926
park_guell.unesco_status: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' (reference 320-001), inscribed 1984
park_guell.status: Completed, operates as a public park; the Monumental Zone (main terrace, mosaics, viaducts, entrance) has required a paid ticket since October 2013, though Barcelona residents enter free
notable_facts: Originally conceived by Güell as a private, English-style garden-city development of 60 luxury home plots; only one plot ever sold — to Gaudí himself
Features the famous mosaic salamander at the main entrance stairway, popularly known as 'El Drac' ('the dragon'), covered in trencadís and serving as an overflow fountain for the underground cistern

Gaudí lived in the park's show home (designed by Francesc Berenguer i Mestres, now the Gaudí House Museum) from 1906 to 1925 with his father and niece before moving to the Sagrada Família workshop; the house opened as a museum in 1963
Became a municipal garden/park after the private development failed
The park hosted the First Congress of the Catalan Language during its construction

The entrance is marked by two whimsical gatehouses forming the Porter's Lodge pavilion: one originally housed a phone booth, while the other now contains a permanent exhibit of the Barcelona City History Museum (MUHBA)
A network of elevated stone pathways and viaducts designed by Gaudí uses inclined columns of local stone mimicking tree trunks and inverted catenary arches for load-bearing compression
